170: - **FR-011**: System MUST handle ad-hoc cross-metric questions by generating safe deterministic Python or SQL computations and returning interactive charts. All LLM-generated Python code MUST execute inside a restricted sandbox with no filesystem access, no network access, and a strict execution timeout. If execution exceeds the timeout or attempts a forbidden operation, the system MUST return an error rather than a partial or unsafe result.
171: - **FR-012**: System MUST stream step-by-step progress messages to the UI while loading data and performing computations.
172: - **FR-013**: System MUST gracefully explain the 2018 telemetry boundary when a user requests car telemetry from an earlier season, and suggest available historical alternatives.
173: - **FR-014**: System MUST display a collapsible Engineering Trace panel alongside every result, showing the exact SQL query or telemetry parameters used.
174: - **FR-015**: System MUST use official F1 team colors (sourced from a canonical registry, not hardcoded) for all driver and team visual encodings, correct for the depicted season.

176: - **FR-017**: System MUST render all telemetry visualizations on a dark HUD background (#0B0F17) with WCAG AA compliant text contrast.
177: - **FR-018**: System MUST provide winner and championship predictions grounded in computed statistics (recent form, circuit history, qualifying pace) with explicit confidence factors and traceable computation sources.
178: - **FR-019**: System MUST provide race-engineer style natural-language commentary on telemetry comparisons, grounded exclusively in the computed metrics.
179: - **FR-020**: System MUST correctly identify corners by famous nickname (e.g., Copse, Eau Rouge, Maggotts-Becketts, 130R, Parabolica) and map them to the correct track coordinates.
180: - **FR-021**: System MUST slice telemetry data for corner comparisons using an entry-apex-exit window of approximately ±200 meters around the corner reference point.
181: - **FR-022**: All interactive charts MUST support hover tooltips, zoom, and pan interactions.
182: - **FR-023**: System MUST require user authentication (sign-in) before granting access to any feature. Unauthenticated users MUST be redirected to a login screen.

186: ### Key Entities
187: 
188: - **Driver**: A Formula 1 driver identified by code, full name, nationality, and career span. Associated with one or more Constructors per season.
189: - **Constructor**: A Formula 1 team identified by name, nationality, and active seasons. Associated with one or two Drivers per season and a team color palette per season.
190: - **Race / Grand Prix**: A race event identified by name, circuit, season year, round number, and date. Contains Results, Lap Times, Pit Stops, and optionally Telemetry Sessions.
191: - **Session**: A specific track session (FP1, FP2, FP3, Qualifying, Sprint, Race) within a Grand Prix weekend. For 2018+ sessions, may contain car Telemetry data.
192: - **Telemetry Lap**: A single timed lap within a Session, containing channel data (Speed, Throttle, Brake, Gear, RPM, DRS, X/Y/Z position) at sub-second intervals.
193: - **Corner / Turn**: A defined section of a Circuit identified by turn number and optionally a famous nickname. Used as the reference point for entry-apex-exit slicing.
194: - **Stint**: A contiguous run of laps on the same tyre compound within a Race, bounded by pit stops or session start/end.
195: - **User Account**: An authenticated identity with a unique identifier, used to gate access to PitWall AI. Associated with a login method (email/password, OAuth, or similar).
196: - **Conversation Session**: A single continuous interaction session between a user and PitWall AI. Contains a rolling summary of earlier turns plus the last 4–6 turns verbatim for context resolution. Not persisted after the session ends.
197: - **Prediction**: A data-driven projection of race or championship outcomes, containing ranked candidates, confidence scores, and the statistical factors that produced them.

27: # PitWall AI Constitution
28: 
29: ## Core Principles
30: 
31: ### I. Zero-Hallucination Math (NON-NEGOTIABLE)
32: 
33: The LLM MUST NEVER calculate statistics, averages, braking points, lap deltas,
34: or any numerical result from memory, training data, or parametric inference.
35: 
36: - Every number displayed to the user MUST originate from one of exactly two
37:   computation paths:
38:   1. **DuckDB SQL** — deterministic queries against structured race data.
39:   2. **Python / NumPy** — deterministic telemetry calculations executed at
40:      runtime against loaded car telemetry arrays.
41: - If a computation path cannot be executed (missing data, query failure), the
42:   system MUST surface an explicit error rather than fabricate or approximate a
43:   value.
44: - The LLM's role is to *author* SQL and Python code, *interpret* returned
45:   results in natural language, and *never* substitute its own arithmetic.
46: - Any code path that produces a user-facing number MUST be traceable to a
47:   SQL query string or a Python/NumPy function invocation with deterministic
48:   inputs.
49: 
50: **Rationale**: Formula 1 strategy decisions depend on sub-tenth-of-a-second
51: precision. A hallucinated delta or braking point can mislead analysis and
52: erode trust in the entire platform.
53: 
54: ### II. Data Domain Separation
55: 
56: A strict boundary MUST be maintained between the two canonical data domains:
57: 
58: | Domain | Source | Coverage | Storage |
59: |---|---|---|---|
60: | Historical Race Data | Ergast / official F1 results | 1950 – 2024+ | DuckDB |
61: | Car Telemetry | FastF1 API | 2018+ | In-memory / parquet cache |
62: 
63: - Queries and computations MUST NOT conflate data from different domains in a
64:   single result without explicitly labeling which domain each datum originates
65:   from.
66: - Historical queries against seasons before 2018 MUST NOT reference telemetry
67:   columns; telemetry queries MUST NOT reference historical-only tables as if
68:   they contain channel data.
69: - When a user request spans both domains (e.g., "Compare Senna's 1991 wins
70:   with Verstappen's 2023 telemetry"), the response MUST clearly demarcate
71:   which portion is historical SQL and which is FastF1 telemetry.
72: 
73: **Rationale**: Mixing heterogeneous data sources without explicit provenance
74: creates invisible accuracy failures and misleading cross-era comparisons.
75: 
76: ### III. Telemetry HUD Visual Standards
77: 
78: All telemetry visualizations MUST render on a dark HUD background using the
79: canonical base color `#0B0F17`.
80: 
81: - Chart backgrounds, panel backgrounds, and dashboard canvases MUST use
82:   `#0B0F17` or a shade within ±5 lightness units in OKLCH space.
83: - Foreground text MUST maintain a minimum WCAG AA contrast ratio (4.5:1)
84:   against the HUD background.
85: - Grid lines, axis labels, and secondary chrome MUST use muted variants that
86:   do not compete with data traces.
87: - No telemetry chart or dashboard panel MAY use a white or light background.
88: 
89: **Rationale**: A consistent dark cockpit aesthetic reinforces the
90: professional motorsport-engineering identity, reduces eye strain during
91: long analysis sessions, and maximizes contrast for thin telemetry traces.
92: 
93: ### IV. Provenance Transparency
94: 
95: Every feature that surfaces data to the user MUST display its provenance

# Research: PitWall AI — F1 Race Engineer

**Feature**: 001-pitwall-ai | **Date**: 2026-11-22

All technical decisions were provided by the user. No NEEDS CLARIFICATION items remain. This document consolidates the rationale for each choice.

## R1: LLM Orchestration Framework

**Decision**: Google ADK (`google-adk`) with Gemini 2.5 Flash

**Rationale**: Google ADK provides a structured agent framework with native tool-calling, function declarations, and streaming support. Gemini 2.5 Flash offers fast inference with strong code-generation capabilities at low cost — ideal for SQL/Python authoring where the model writes code rather than performing arithmetic. The ADK's tool-routing pattern naturally enforces the zero-hallucination boundary: the LLM selects and parameterizes tools, but never computes numbers itself.

**Alternatives Considered**:
- LangChain/LangGraph: More ecosystem momentum but heavier abstraction; ADK is leaner and natively aligned with Gemini.
- OpenAI function calling: Would require a separate API key and billing; ADK keeps the stack on a single provider.
- Direct Gemini API calls: Would work but ADK adds tool declaration, session management, and streaming helpers that reduce boilerplate.

## R2: Historical Data Storage

**Decision**: DuckDB with Kaggle CSV ingestion, `\N` → NULL normalization, read-only SQL views

**Rationale**: DuckDB is an embedded analytical database that requires zero infrastructure (no server process). It excels at analytical queries over CSV-scale data (~100K–1M rows). The `\N` sentinel used in Ergast/Kaggle CSVs must be normalized to SQL NULL at ingestion time to prevent silent type errors. Read-only views (`v_race_results`, `v_qualifying`, `v_pit_stops`, `v_driver_standings`) provide a stable query interface and prevent accidental writes — enforcing Constitution Principle I (all numbers from SQL).

**Alternatives Considered**:
- SQLite: Lacks analytical query optimizations (columnar scans, vectorized execution) that DuckDB provides.
- PostgreSQL: Requires a running server process; overkill for 5–10 concurrent users with static historical data.
- Pandas-only: No SQL interface for the LLM to generate queries against; would require the LLM to write Python data manipulation code instead, increasing hallucination surface.

**Key Implementation Details**:
- Ingestion script reads all CSVs from `data/kaggle_csvs/`, replaces `\N` strings with NULL during COPY.
- Views are created at startup via `CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW` statements.
- DuckDB connection is opened in read-only mode for query execution tools; write access only during initial ingestion.

## R3: Car Telemetry Pipeline

**Decision**: FastF1 with persistent disk cache (`./data/fastf1_cache`) + NumPy 1-meter distance interpolation

**Rationale**: FastF1 is the de-facto Python library for accessing F1 telemetry data (2018+). Its built-in caching avoids re-downloading large session files. NumPy 1-meter distance interpolation resamples telemetry channels to a uniform spatial grid, which is essential for accurate corner slicing (±200m entry-apex-exit windows) and driver-to-driver comparison — you can't compare two drivers' speed at "the same point on track" without spatial alignment.

**Alternatives Considered**:
- Raw F1 timing API: No public stable API; FastF1 abstracts this.
- Time-based interpolation: Would misalign traces through corners where drivers have different speeds (and thus cover distance at different rates). Distance-based is correct for spatial comparisons.

**Key Implementation Details**:
- `fastf1.Cache.enable_cache('./data/fastf1_cache')` at app startup.
- Cache-first fallback: check cache before network call; on transient timeout, retry 1–2 times; fail with error if uncached.
- Interpolation: `np.interp()` to resample Speed, Throttle, Brake, Gear, RPM, DRS onto a 1-meter distance grid per lap.

## R4: Corner Identification & Slicing

**Decision**: Curated `data/corner_nicknames.json` + fuzzy entity resolver

**Rationale**: Corner nicknames (Eau Rouge, Copse, 130R, Parabolica, Maggotts-Becketts) are culturally significant but have no programmatic standard. A curated JSON mapping provides deterministic, auditable corner-to-turn-number resolution. The fuzzy resolver handles spelling variations and partial matches. The ±200m entry-apex-exit slicing window is defined per corner based on the JSON metadata.

**JSON Structure**:
```json
{
  "silverstone": {
    "circuit_key": "silverstone",
    "corners": {
      "copse": { "turn_number": 9, "distance_m": 2340 },
      "maggotts": { "turn_number": 11, "distance_m": 2890 },
      "becketts": { "turn_number": 12, "distance_m": 3050 },
      "stowe": { "turn_number": 15, "distance_m": 4200 }
    }
  },
  "spa": {
    "circuit_key": "spa",
    "corners": {
      "eau_rouge": { "turn_number": 3, "distance_m": 850 },
      "raidillon": { "turn_number": 4, "distance_m": 1020 }
    }
  }
}
```

**Alternatives Considered**:
- Automatic corner detection from curvature: Unreliable for complex corner sequences (Maggotts-Becketts) and requires GPS coordinate processing per circuit.
- Hardcoded turn numbers in source: Not maintainable or auditable; JSON is easier to extend.

## R5: Visualization Strategy

**Decision**: Plotly JSON builders (backend) + react-plotly.js (frontend), two-tier system

**Rationale**: Plotly's JSON-serializable figure format allows the backend to construct complete chart specifications (including the dark HUD theme, team colors, axis labels) and send them to the frontend as JSON over SSE. react-plotly.js renders them interactively with zero additional chart logic on the client. The two-tier system:
- **Tier 1 (Preset charts)**: Backend Python functions build Plotly JSON for known chart types (corner comparison, full-lap overlay, stint degradation, position evolution, historical bar/line/table). These are deterministic and testable.
- **Tier 2 (Ad-hoc charts)**: The LLM generates Python code that uses Plotly to build a figure; this code runs in the timeout-guarded sandbox. The sandbox has access to DuckDB query results and NumPy but no filesystem or network.

**Alternatives Considered**:
- D3.js: Maximum flexibility but requires significant frontend charting code; Plotly provides interactive charts with minimal client code.
- Chart.js: Lacks the multi-subplot support needed for synchronized telemetry panels (Speed + Throttle + Brake + Gear).
- Matplotlib: Server-side rasterization produces static images, not interactive charts.

## R6: Streaming Architecture

**Decision**: FastAPI SSE via `/api/chat/stream` endpoint

**Rationale**: Server-Sent Events (SSE) provide a simple, HTTP-native streaming mechanism that works with standard browser `EventSource` API. Each SSE event carries a typed payload: `status` (progress messages), `text` (LLM commentary), `chart` (Plotly JSON), `trace` (Engineering Trace data), `error`. This maps cleanly to the streaming progress requirement (FR-012) and allows the frontend to render incremental results.

**Alternatives Considered**:
- WebSockets: Bidirectional, but the client only needs to send one message (the question); SSE is simpler for server-push patterns.
- Long polling: Higher latency and more complex client logic.
- gRPC streaming: Would require a gRPC client in the browser (gRPC-web), adding complexity.

## R7: Authentication

**Decision**: Session-based authentication with sign-in required

**Rationale**: The app requires authentication (FR-023) for all features. For 5–10 concurrent users, a simple session-based auth with JWT tokens is sufficient. OAuth integration can be added later. Sessions are stateless across browser sessions (FR-025) — conversation context is not persisted.

## R8: Ad-Hoc Python Sandbox

**Decision**: Timeout-guarded restricted `exec()` with controlled globals

**Rationale**: FR-011 requires safe execution of LLM-generated Python. The sandbox provides a restricted `exec()` environment with:
- Allowed imports: `numpy`, `pandas`, `plotly`, `math`, `statistics`, `datetime`
- No filesystem access (`open`, `os`, `pathlib` blocked)
- No network access (`requests`, `urllib`, `socket` blocked)
- No subprocess/system calls
- Execution timeout (configurable, default 30s)
- Pre-injected variables: query results (DataFrames), DuckDB connection (read-only)

**Alternatives Considered**:
- Docker container per execution: Secure but adds 2–5s container startup latency; overkill for 5–10 users.
- WebAssembly sandbox (Pyodide): Would require shipping Python runtime to the browser; unnecessary when backend can sandbox.
- Restricted AST analysis: Too brittle; timeout + controlled globals is simpler and more robust.

## R9: Entity Resolution

**Decision**: Fuzzy driver/circuit resolver using string similarity matching

**Rationale**: Users type driver names and circuit names in natural language with varying specificity ("Max", "Verstappen", "Max Verstappen", "VER"). A fuzzy resolver uses string similarity (Levenshtein distance or token-based matching) to map user input to canonical driver codes and circuit identifiers in the DuckDB database. This bridges the gap between natural language and the structured data model.

**Key Implementation Details**:
- Driver resolver: matches against full name, surname, and 3-letter code from DuckDB `drivers` table.
- Circuit resolver: matches against circuit name, location, and country.
- Corner resolver: matches against `corner_nicknames.json` entries.
- Confidence threshold: matches below a configurable similarity score trigger a disambiguation prompt.

## R10: Frontend Architecture

**Decision**: React + TypeScript + Vite + Tailwind CSS + react-plotly.js

**Rationale**: React provides component-based UI composition. TypeScript adds type safety for the SSE event contracts. Vite offers fast HMR during development. Tailwind CSS enables the dark pit-wall aesthetic with utility classes. react-plotly.js renders Plotly JSON figures with built-in interactivity (hover, zoom, pan). The layout is a two-panel design: chat + preset prompts on the left, interactive Plotly stage + collapsible Engineering Trace drawer on the right.

**Dark HUD Theme**:
- Background: `#0B0F17` (Tailwind custom color `pitwall-bg`)
- Text: `#E2E8F0` (slate-200, 12.6:1 contrast ratio vs #0B0F17)
- Muted: `#64748B` (slate-500, for grid lines and secondary chrome)
- Accent: Team colors from FastF1 at runtime

# API Contracts: PitWall AI

**Feature**: 001-pitwall-ai | **Date**: 2026-11-22

## Base URL

```
http://localhost:8000/api
```

## Authentication

### POST /api/auth/login

Authenticate a user and receive a session token.

**Request Body**:
```json
{
  "email": "user@example.com",
  "password": "REDACTED"
}
```

**Response 200**:
```json
{
  "token": "REDACTED",
  "user": {
    "id": "uuid-REDACTED",
    "email": "user@example.com"
  }
}
```

**Response 401**:
```json
{
  "error": "Invalid credentials"
}
```

### POST /api/auth/logout

Invalidate the current session.

**Headers**: `Authorization: Bearer <token>`

**Response 200**:
```json
{
  "message": "Logged out"
}
```

## Chat (Streaming)

### POST /api/chat/stream

Submit a natural-language F1 question and receive a streaming SSE response.

**Headers**: `Authorization: Bearer <token>`

**Request Body**:
```json
{
  "message": "Compare Verstappen and Leclerc through Eau Rouge at the 2023 Belgian GP",
  "session_id": "uuid-REDACTED-or-null"
}
```

- `session_id`: If null, creates a new conversation session. If provided, continues the existing session with multi-turn context.

**Response**: `text/event-stream` (SSE)

Each SSE event has the format:
```
event: <event_type>
data: <json_payload>

```

#### SSE Event Types

**`session`** — Emitted first, provides the session ID:
```json
{
  "session_id": "uuid-REDACTED"
}
```

**`status`** — Progress updates during data loading/computation:
```json
{
  "step": "Loading 2023 Belgian GP Qualifying session…",
  "progress": 0.3
}
```

**`text`** — LLM natural-language commentary (streamed token-by-token or in chunks):
```json
{
  "content": "Verstappen brakes 12 meters later than Leclerc into Eau Rouge...",
  "is_complete": false
}
```

**`chart`** — Plotly JSON figure ready for rendering:
```json
{
  "chart_id": "corner-comparison-speed",
  "chart_type": "corner_comparison | full_lap | stint_degradation | position_evolution | historical | adhoc",
  "plotly_json": {
    "data": [...],
    "layout": {...}
  },
  "metadata": {
    "grand_prix": "Belgian Grand Prix",
    "year": 2023,
    "session": "Qualifying",
    "drivers": ["VER", "LEC"],
    "laps": [1, 1],
    "compounds": ["SOFT", "SOFT"],
    "weather": "Dry"
  }
}
```

**`trace`** — Engineering Trace data for provenance transparency:
```json
{
  "domain": "telemetry | historical | both",
  "sql_query": "SELECT ... FROM v_race_results WHERE ...",
  "telemetry_params": {
    "year": 2023,
    "grand_prix": "Belgian Grand Prix",
    "session": "Q",
    "drivers": ["VER", "LEC"],
    "corner": "Eau Rouge",
    "turn_number": 3,
    "slice_range_m": 200
  },
  "computed_metrics": {
    "braking_point_delta_m": 12.3,
    "apex_min_speed_ver_kph": 285.4,
    "apex_min_speed_lec_kph": 282.1,
    "lowest_gear_ver": 5,
    "lowest_gear_lec": 5,
    "full_throttle_pickup_delta_m": -4.7,
    "corner_time_delta_s": 0.047
  },
  "python_snippet": "# Sandbox execution code (if ad-hoc)"
}
```

**`error`** — Error event:
```json
{
  "error": "Car telemetry data is available from the 2018 season onwards.",
  "suggestion": "For 2004 and earlier seasons, I can provide historical race results, lap times, and championship standings.",
  "error_type": "data_boundary | data_unavailable | sandbox_timeout | query_error"
}
```

**`done`** — Stream complete:
```json
{
  "total_time_ms": 8432
}
```

#### Stream Sequence (Typical)

```
event: session
data: {"session_id": "abc-123"}

event: status
data: {"step": "Loading 2023 Belgian GP Qualifying…", "progress": 0.1}

event: status
data: {"step": "Extracting VER fastest lap…", "progress": 0.3}

event: status
data: {"step": "Slicing Eau Rouge corridor (±200m)…", "progress": 0.5}

event: status
data: {"step": "Computing corner metrics…", "progress": 0.7}

event: chart
data: {"chart_id": "corner-speed", "chart_type": "corner_comparison", ...}

event: chart
data: {"chart_id": "corner-minimap", "chart_type": "corner_comparison", ...}

event: trace
data: {"domain": "telemetry", "telemetry_params": {...}, "computed_metrics": {...}}

event: text
data: {"content": "Verstappen brakes 12.3m later...", "is_complete": true}

event: done
data: {"total_time_ms": 8432}
```

## Health

### GET /api/health

Health check endpoint (no auth required).

**Response 200**:
```json
{
  "status": "healthy",
  "duckdb": "connected",
  "fastf1_cache": "available",
  "version": "0.1.0"
}
```

## Error Responses (Global)

All endpoints return errors in a consistent format:

| Status | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| 401 | Missing or invalid authentication token |
| 422 | Invalid request body (validation error) |
| 500 | Internal server error |

```json
{
  "error": "Human-readable error message",
  "error_type": "auth_required | validation_error | internal_error"
}
```

### Source Tables (from CSV ingestion)

#### circuits

### Read-Only SQL Views

#### v_race_results

Joins results + races + drivers + constructors + circuits + status. Provides a single denormalized view for all race result queries.

```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW v_race_results AS
SELECT
    r.year, r.round, r.name AS grand_prix, r.date AS race_date,
    c.name AS circuit, c.country,
    d.code AS driver_code, d.forename, d.surname, d.nationality AS driver_nationality,
    con.name AS constructor, con.nationality AS constructor_nationality,
    res.grid, res.position, res.positionText, res.points, res.laps,
    res.time AS finish_time, res.milliseconds AS finish_ms,
    res.fastestLap, res.fastestLapTime, res.fastestLapSpeed,
    s.status
FROM results res
JOIN races r ON res.raceId = r.raceId
JOIN drivers d ON res.driverId = d.driverId
JOIN constructors con ON res.constructorId = con.constructorId
JOIN circuits c ON r.circuitId = c.circuitId
JOIN status s ON res.statusId = s.statusId;
```

#### v_qualifying

```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW v_qualifying AS
SELECT
    r.year, r.round, r.name AS grand_prix,
    d.code AS driver_code, d.forename, d.surname,
    con.name AS constructor,
    q.position, q.q1, q.q2, q.q3
FROM qualifying q
JOIN races r ON q.raceId = r.raceId
JOIN drivers d ON q.driverId = d.driverId
JOIN constructors con ON q.constructorId = con.constructorId;
```

#### v_pit_stops

```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW v_pit_stops AS
SELECT
    r.year, r.round, r.name AS grand_prix,
    d.code AS driver_code, d.surname,
    con.name AS constructor,
    ps.stop, ps.lap, ps.duration, ps.milliseconds AS duration_ms
FROM pit_stops ps
JOIN races r ON ps.raceId = r.raceId
JOIN drivers d ON ps.driverId = d.driverId
JOIN constructors con ON (
    SELECT res.constructorId FROM results res
    WHERE res.raceId = ps.raceId AND res.driverId = ps.driverId
    LIMIT 1
) = con.constructorId;
```

#### v_driver_standings

```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW v_driver_standings AS
SELECT
    r.year, r.round, r.name AS grand_prix,
    d.code AS driver_code, d.forename, d.surname,
    ds.points, ds.position, ds.wins
FROM driver_standings ds
JOIN races r ON ds.raceId = r.raceId
JOIN drivers d ON ds.driverId = d.driverId;
```

---

## Chat (SSE Streaming)

### POST /api/chat/stream

Send a natural-language question and receive a streaming response via Server-Sent Events.

**Headers**:
```
Authorization: Bearer <JWT token>
Content-Type: application/json
Accept: text/event-stream
```

**Request Body**:
```json
{
  "message": "REDACTED",
  "session_id": "REDACTED (UUID, optional — omit to start new session)"
}
```

**Response**: `text/event-stream` with the following event types:

#### Event: `session`
Emitted once at the start. Provides the session ID for follow-up messages.
```
event: session
data: {"session_id": "uuid-REDACTED"}
```

#### Event: `status`
Emitted during data loading/computation. Provides streaming progress messages.
```
event: status
data: {"message": "Loading 2023 Belgian GP Qualifying session…"}
```

#### Event: `text`
Emitted for natural-language commentary from the AI race engineer.
```
event: text
data: {"content": "Verstappen brakes 12 meters later than Leclerc into Eau Rouge…", "done": false}
```
When `done: true`, the text stream is complete.

#### Event: `chart`
Emitted when a Plotly visualization is ready. Contains a complete Plotly JSON figure.
```
event: chart
data: {
  "chart_id": "REDACTED",
  "chart_type": "corner_comparison | full_lap | stint_degradation | position_evolution | historical | adhoc",
  "title": "Speed Comparison: VER vs LEC — Eau Rouge (2023 Belgian GP Q)",
  "plotly_json": { <complete Plotly figure JSON> },
  "metadata": {
    "grand_prix": "Belgian Grand Prix",
    "year": 2023,
    "session": "Qualifying",
    "drivers": ["VER", "LEC"],
    "laps": [1, 1],
    "compounds": ["SOFT", "SOFT"],
    "weather": "Dry"
  }
}
```

#### Event: `trace`
Emitted with provenance data for the Engineering Trace panel.
```
event: trace
data: {
  "domain": "historical_sql | telemetry | hybrid",
  "sql_query": "SELECT ... FROM v_race_results WHERE ...",
  "telemetry_params": {
    "year": 2023,
    "grand_prix": "Belgian Grand Prix",
    "session": "Q",
    "drivers": ["VER", "LEC"],
    "laps": [1, 1],
    "channels": ["Speed", "Throttle", "Brake", "nGear"],
    "corner": "Eau Rouge",
    "slice_range_m": [-200, 200]
  },
  "python_code": "# (only for ad-hoc Tier 2 charts)\nimport numpy as np\n..."
}
```

#### Event: `error`
Emitted on failure.
```
event: error
data: {
  "error": "REDACTED",
  "error_type": "data_unavailable | boundary_2018 | timeout | sandbox_violation | auth_expired | unknown",
  "suggestion": "REDACTED (optional — alternative analysis suggestion)"
}
```

#### Event: `done`
Emitted once at the end of the response. Signals the client to close the SSE connection.
```
event: done
data: {}
```

---

## Health Check

### GET /api/health

**Response 200**:
```json
{
  "status": "ok",
  "duckdb": "connected",
  "fastf1_cache": "ready",
  "tables_loaded": 10,
  "views_created": 4
}
```

---

## SSE Event Type Summary

| Event | Purpose | Cardinality |
|-------|---------|-------------|
| `session` | Provide session ID | Exactly once |
| `status` | Streaming progress | 0–N |
| `text` | AI commentary | 1–N (last has `done: true`) |
| `chart` | Plotly visualization | 0–N |
| `trace` | Engineering Trace | Exactly once |
| `error` | Error information | 0–1 |
| `done` | End of response | Exactly once |

## Error Codes

| error_type | HTTP Context | Description |
|------------|--------------|-------------|
| `data_unavailable` | 200 (SSE) | Requested data not found in DuckDB or FastF1 |
| `boundary_2018` | 200 (SSE) | Telemetry requested for pre-2018 season |
| `timeout` | 200 (SSE) | Sandbox execution or FastF1 load exceeded timeout |
| `sandbox_violation` | 200 (SSE) | Ad-hoc Python attempted forbidden operation |
| `auth_expired` | 401 | JWT token expired or invalid |
| `unknown` | 200 (SSE) | Unexpected server error |

## Request/Response Size Limits

- Maximum message length: 2000 characters
- Maximum Plotly JSON payload: 5 MB per chart event
- SSE connection timeout: 120 seconds (covers worst-case telemetry load + computation)

# Quickstart Validation Guide: PitWall AI

**Feature**: 001-pitwall-ai | **Date**: 2026-11-22

This guide provides runnable validation scenarios that prove each core capability works end-to-end. See [data-model.md](./data-model.md) for entity details and [contracts/api-contracts.md](./contracts/api-contracts.md) for API specifications.

## Prerequisites

- Python 3.12+
- Node.js 20+ and pnpm
- Kaggle F1 dataset CSVs in `backend/data/kaggle_csvs/`
- Internet access for initial FastF1 cache population (subsequent runs use disk cache)

## Setup Commands

### Backend

```bash
cd backend
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate   # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -r requirements.txt

# Ingest Kaggle CSVs into DuckDB (creates data/f1_data.duckdb)
python -m app.data.duckdb_manager

# Enable FastF1 cache
mkdir -p data/fastf1_cache
```

### Frontend

```bash
cd frontend
pnpm install
```

## Validation Scenarios

### V1: DuckDB Ingestion & \N Normalization

**What it proves**: Kaggle CSVs are correctly loaded with `\N` → NULL normalization. Read-only SQL views return accurate data.

**Run**:
```bash
cd backend
pytest tests/test_duckdb_ingestion.py -v
```

**Expected Outcome**:
- All `\N` values in source CSVs are stored as SQL NULL (not the string `\N`).
- `v_race_results` returns Max Verstappen as 2023 Bahrain GP winner.
- `v_qualifying` returns correct Q1/Q2/Q3 times for a known session.
- `v_pit_stops` returns correct pit stop counts and durations.
- `v_driver_standings` returns correct cumulative points.

### V2: Read-Only SQL Guardrails

**What it proves**: The SQL execution tool rejects all write operations, preventing data corruption.

**Run**:
```bash
cd backend
pytest tests/test_sql_guardrails.py -v
```

**Expected Outcome**:
- `INSERT INTO results ...` → rejected with error.
- `UPDATE drivers SET ...` → rejected with error.
- `DELETE FROM races ...` → rejected with error.
- `DROP TABLE results` → rejected with error.
- `SELECT * FROM v_race_results WHERE year = 2023` → succeeds with results.

### V3: Corner Slicing Math

**What it proves**: Telemetry interpolation and corner slicing produce correct metrics using the 2024 British GP Qualifying fixture.

**Run**:
```bash
cd backend
pytest tests/test_corner_slicing.py -v
```

**Expected Outcome**:
- Telemetry is interpolated to 1-meter distance grid.
- Corner window (±200m around Copse) correctly slices entry-apex-exit zone.
- Braking point delta, apex min speed, lowest gear, full-throttle pickup, and corner time delta are computed and match manually verified values from the same FastF1 data.
- GPS coordinates within the corner window are correct for mini-map rendering.

### V4: Entity Resolution

**What it proves**: Fuzzy matching correctly resolves natural-language driver/circuit/corner names.

**Run**:
```bash
cd backend
pytest tests/test_entity_resolver.py -v
```

**Expected Outcome**:
- "Verstappen" → `VER`, "Max" → `VER`, "max verstappen" → `VER`.
- "Silverstone" → correct circuit ID, "British Grand Prix" → correct circuit ID.
- "Copse" → Turn 9 at Silverstone, "Eau Rouge" → Turn 3 at Spa.
- Ambiguous input (e.g., just "Turn 3") prompts for circuit disambiguation.

### V5: Full Backend Integration (SSE Stream)

**What it proves**: The full pipeline — from natural-language input through LLM tool routing to Plotly chart output — works end-to-end with correct SSE events.

**Run**:
```bash
cd backend
# Start the server
uvicorn app.main:app --port 8000 &

# Test a historical query
curl -N -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/chat/stream \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <test-token>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"message": "Who won the 2023 Bahrain Grand Prix?"}'
```

**Expected Outcome**:
- SSE events arrive in order: `session` → `status` (1+) → `text` → `chart` → `trace` → `done`.
- `text` event contains "Max Verstappen" (or equivalent).
- `trace` event contains the exact SQL query executed.
- `chart` event contains valid Plotly JSON with dark HUD theme.

### V6: Frontend Smoke Test (Playwright)

**What it proves**: The React frontend renders Plotly charts correctly with zero console errors on the dark HUD background.

**Run**:
```bash
# Start backend
cd backend && uvicorn app.main:app --port 8000 &

# Start frontend
cd frontend && pnpm dev &

# Run Playwright
cd frontend && pnpm exec playwright test tests/smoke.spec.ts
```

**Expected Outcome**:
- Login page renders and accepts credentials.
- After login, the pit-wall layout renders (chat panel left, chart stage right).
- Submitting a test query produces a Plotly chart in the chart stage.
- The Engineering Trace drawer is accessible and shows query/telemetry params.
- Zero JavaScript console errors throughout the test.
- Background color of chart stage is `#0B0F17`.

### V7: Full pytest Suite

**What it proves**: All backend tests pass against real data fixtures.

**Run**:
```bash
cd backend
pytest -v --tb=short
```

**Expected Outcome**:
- All tests in `test_duckdb_ingestion.py`, `test_sql_guardrails.py`, `test_corner_slicing.py`, `test_entity_resolver.py`, `test_telemetry_tools.py`, `test_chart_builders.py`, and `test_prediction.py` pass.
- No synthetic mocks used for user-facing numerical computations.

# PitWall AI — Agent Context & Rules

## Project Overview
**PitWall AI** is an AI Race Engineer web application that answers natural-language Formula 1 questions spanning 1950 to 2024+ with interactive Plotly visualizations.

- **Active Feature**: `001-pitwall-ai` ([specs/001-pitwall-ai/spec.md](specs/001-pitwall-ai/spec.md))
- **Implementation Plan**: [specs/001-pitwall-ai/plan.md](specs/001-pitwall-ai/plan.md)
- **Constitution**: [.specify/memory/constitution.md](.specify/memory/constitution.md)

---

## Non-Negotiable Constitution Principles

1. **Zero-Hallucination Math**:
   - The LLM MUST NEVER calculate statistics, averages, braking points, or lap deltas from memory or parametric weights.
   - Every number displayed to the user MUST originate from DuckDB SQL queries or deterministic Python/NumPy calculations.
2. **Data Domain Separation**:
   - Historical Race Data (1950–2024+): DuckDB SQL views (`v_race_results`, `v_qualifying`, `v_pit_stops`, `v_driver_standings`).
   - Car Telemetry (2018+): FastF1 API with persistent disk cache (`./data/fastf1_cache`) and NumPy 1-meter distance interpolation.
   - Clear boundary explanation MUST be provided if pre-2018 car telemetry is requested.
3. **Telemetry HUD Visual Standards**:
   - All charts, panels, and dashboard canvases MUST use the dark HUD background `#0B0F17`.
   - Text contrast MUST meet WCAG AA (4.5:1 minimum).
4. **Provenance Transparency**:
   - Every result MUST supply Engineering Trace data (exact SQL query or FastF1 session/lap/driver/channel parameters).
5. **Automated Verification**:
   - All features MUST be backed by pytest suites validating against real race data fixtures (no synthetic mocks for user-facing numbers).
6. **Official F1 Team Colors**:
   - Team colors MUST be retrieved dynamically from `fastf1.plotting.get_team_color()` for the specific season, never hardcoded.
7. **Session & Lap Metadata Fidelity**:
   - Grand Prix name, season year, session type, lap number, driver code, compound, and weather MUST be shown on all visualizations.

---

## Technical Stack & Architecture

### Backend (`backend/`)
- **Runtime**: Python 3.12+
- **Framework**: FastAPI with SSE streaming endpoint at `POST /api/chat/stream`
- **Orchestration**: Google ADK (`google-adk`) using `gemini-2.5-flash` for agent tool routing
- **Historical Data**: DuckDB (`data/f1_data.duckdb`) ingesting Kaggle CSVs (`data/kaggle_csvs/`) with `\N` → `NULL` normalization and curated read-only views
- **Car Telemetry**: FastF1 with disk cache at `./data/fastf1_cache` + NumPy 1-meter spatial interpolation for corner slicing (±200m around corner reference points)
- **Entity Resolution**: Fuzzy driver/circuit name matching + `data/corner_nicknames.json`
- **Visualizations**: Plotly JSON builders (Tier 1 preset figures + Tier 2 restricted Python sandbox for ad-hoc queries)
- **Authentication**: JWT session tokens; users must sign in; stateless across browser sessions (last 4–6 turns verbatim + rolling summary within a session)

### Frontend (`frontend/`)
- **Framework**: React 18+ with TypeScript and Vite
- **Styling**: Tailwind CSS configured with `#0B0F17` HUD background (`pitwall-bg`)
- **Charts**: `react-plotly.js` rendering backend-supplied Plotly figures
- **Layout**: Two-panel dark pit-wall interface (chat + preset prompts left; interactive Plotly stage + collapsible Engineering Trace drawer right)

### Testing
- **Backend**: `pytest` covering DuckDB `\N` ingestion, read-only SQL guardrails, corner-slicing math (2024 British GP Qualifying fixture), and prediction factor traceability
- **Frontend**: Playwright E2E smoke test verifying Plotly rendering and zero console errors

---

## Artifact Index (Feature `001-pitwall-ai`)

- **Feature Spec**: [`specs/001-pitwall-ai/spec.md`](specs/001-pitwall-ai/spec.md)
- **Implementation Plan**: [`specs/001-pitwall-ai/plan.md`](specs/001-pitwall-ai/plan.md)
- **Research & Decisions**: [`specs/001-pitwall-ai/research.md`](specs/001-pitwall-ai/research.md)
- **Data Model**: [`specs/001-pitwall-ai/data-model.md`](specs/001-pitwall-ai/data-model.md)
- **API Contracts**: [`specs/001-pitwall-ai/contracts/api-contracts.md`](specs/001-pitwall-ai/contracts/api-contracts.md)
- **Quickstart Guide**: [`specs/001-pitwall-ai/quickstart.md`](specs/001-pitwall-ai/quickstart.md)
- **Spec Quality Checklist**: [`specs/001-pitwall-ai/checklists/requirements.md`](specs/001-pitwall-ai/checklists/requirements.md)

1: # Feature Specification: PitWall AI — F1 Race Engineer
2: 
3: **Feature Branch**: `001-pitwall-ai`

9: **Input**: User description: "Build PitWall AI, an AI Race Engineer web app that answers natural-language Formula 1 questions from 1950 to 2024+ with interactive visualizations."
10: 
11: ## User Scenarios & Testing *(mandatory)*
12: 
13: ### User Story 1 - Historical F1 Question Answering (Priority: P1)
14: 
15: A user opens PitWall AI, types a natural-language question about Formula 1 history (e.g., "How many wins did Ayrton Senna have in 1991?" or "Which constructor has the most championships?"), and receives an accurate answer accompanied by an interactive chart or table and the exact SQL query that produced the data.
16: 
17: **Why this priority**: This is the broadest-reach capability. It covers 75 years of F1 data (1950–2024+), serves the widest range of questions, and validates the core zero-hallucination pipeline end-to-end: natural language → SQL generation → query execution → result visualization.
18: 
19: **Independent Test**: Can be fully tested by submitting historical questions and verifying answers against official FIA/F1 records. Delivers immediate standalone value.
20: 
21: **Acceptance Scenarios**:
22: 
23: 1. **Given** the user types "Who won the 2023 Bahrain Grand Prix?", **When** the system processes the question, **Then** it returns "Max Verstappen" with a results table showing the top-10 classification, an interactive chart of the finishing order, and a collapsible Engineering Trace panel displaying the exact DuckDB SQL query executed.
24: 2. **Given** the user asks "Show me Lewis Hamilton's podium finishes per season", **When** the system processes the query, **Then** it returns an interactive bar chart with one bar per season, correct podium counts matching official records, and the SQL query visible in the Engineering Trace.
25: 3. **Given** the user asks a question about a driver or race that does not exist in the database, **When** the system cannot find matching data, **Then** it returns a clear "No data found" message rather than fabricating a response.
26: 
27: ---
28: 
29: ### User Story 2 - Corner-by-Corner Telemetry Comparison (Priority: P1)
30: 
31: A user asks to compare two drivers through a specific corner (by turn number or famous nickname like "Eau Rouge," "Copse," or "130R") for a given session. PitWall AI loads the telemetry, slices the entry-apex-exit zone (±200m around the corner), and renders a synchronized multi-panel interactive chart showing Speed, Speed Delta, Throttle, Brake, and Gear traces, plus a zoomed GPS track mini-map colored by which driver is faster. The system defaults to Qualifying fastest laps when the user does not specify a session.
32: 
33: **Why this priority**: This is the signature differentiating feature — no existing public tool offers corner-level comparison with an AI race-engineer explanation. It exercises the full telemetry pipeline and the most complex visualization.
34: 
35: **Independent Test**: Can be tested by requesting a known corner comparison (e.g., "Compare Verstappen and Leclerc through Copse at the 2023 British GP Qualifying") and verifying computed metrics (braking point delta, apex min speed, lowest gear, full-throttle pickup point, corner time delta) against manually computed values from the same FastF1 data.
36: 
37: **Acceptance Scenarios**:
38: 
39: 1. **Given** the user asks "Compare Verstappen and Leclerc through Eau Rouge at the 2023 Belgian GP", **When** the session is not specified, **Then** the system defaults to Qualifying fastest laps, loads FastF1 telemetry, renders the multi-panel chart (Speed, Delta, Throttle, Brake, Gear), displays the GPS mini-map colored by faster driver, computes the five corner metrics, and provides race-engineer commentary grounded in the computed numbers.
40: 2. **Given** the user specifies a turn number instead of a name (e.g., "Turn 7 at Monza"), **When** the system processes the request, **Then** it correctly maps the turn number to the corner coordinates and produces the same comparison output.
41: 3. **Given** telemetry data is not available for the requested session (e.g., a pre-2018 race), **When** the system detects this, **Then** it explains the 2018 boundary for car telemetry data clearly and suggests alternative historical analyses that are available.
42: 
43: ---
44: 
45: ### User Story 3 - Full-Lap Telemetry Overlay (Priority: P2)
46: 
47: A user asks to overlay two drivers' full-lap telemetry for a given session. PitWall AI renders an interactive speed trace, throttle/brake map, and gear usage chart across the entire lap with driver traces colored by official F1 team colors.
48: 
49: **Why this priority**: Full-lap overlays are a natural complement to corner comparisons and serve users who want the big picture before drilling into specific corners. Reuses the same telemetry loading infrastructure.
50: 
51: **Independent Test**: Can be tested by requesting a full-lap overlay for two drivers in a known session and comparing the rendered speed trace against the raw FastF1 channel data.
52: 
53: **Acceptance Scenarios**:
54: 
55: 1. **Given** the user asks "Overlay Verstappen vs Hamilton full lap at 2023 Abu Dhabi Qualifying", **When** the system loads both drivers' fastest qualifying laps, **Then** it renders a synchronized speed trace with correct official team colors, displays lap time and delta, and shows session metadata (GP, year, session type, lap number, compound).
56: 2. **Given** one driver did not set a valid lap in the session, **When** the system detects missing data, **Then** it informs the user which driver's data is unavailable and offers alternative sessions.
57: 
58: ---
59: 
60: ### User Story 4 - Tyre Stint Degradation Analysis (Priority: P2)
61: 
62: A user asks about tyre degradation for a driver during a race. PitWall AI filters out pit-in/pit-out laps and Safety Car laps, then charts lap time progression per stint, colored by compound, with a degradation trend line.
63: 
64: **Why this priority**: Tyre strategy is central to F1 race engineering. This feature builds on the race data pipeline and adds stint-level analysis that is directly actionable for understanding race strategy.
65: 
66: **Independent Test**: Can be tested by loading a known race, verifying that pit laps and Safety Car laps are excluded from the degradation chart, and checking lap times against official timing data.
67: 
68: **Acceptance Scenarios**:
69: 
70: 1. **Given** the user asks "Show me Verstappen's tyre degradation at the 2023 Spanish GP", **When** the system processes the request, **Then** it displays a chart of lap times per stint, colored by tyre compound, with pit and Safety Car laps excluded, a degradation trend line per stint, and session metadata.
71: 2. **Given** a race had a red flag, **When** the system processes the data, **Then** it correctly handles the interrupted session and indicates the red-flag period in the visualization.
72: 
73: ---
74: 
75: ### User Story 5 - Race Position Evolution (Priority: P2)
76: 
77: A user asks to see how race positions changed throughout a Grand Prix. PitWall AI renders a "spaghetti plot" showing each driver's position on each lap, colored by team colors, with key events (pit stops, retirements, Safety Cars) annotated.
78: 
79: **Why this priority**: Position charts are the most common race-analysis visualization in F1 broadcasting and fan communities. They tie together pit strategy and on-track action.
80: 
81: **Independent Test**: Can be tested by rendering a position chart for a known race and verifying final positions against official classification.
82: 
83: **Acceptance Scenarios**:
84: 
85: 1. **Given** the user asks "Show me the race position chart for the 2023 Brazilian GP", **When** the system renders the chart, **Then** each driver's trace uses the correct team color, final positions match the official classification, and pit-stop laps are marked.
86: 2. **Given** the user clicks on a driver's trace, **When** they interact with the chart, **Then** the driver's line is highlighted and a tooltip shows lap-by-lap details.
87: 
88: ---
89: 
90: ### User Story 6 - Ad-Hoc Cross-Metric Analysis (Priority: P3)
91: 
92: A user asks a custom question that does not map to any preset chart type (e.g., "Plot average pit stop duration per team across the last 5 seasons" or "What is the correlation between qualifying position and race finish at Monaco?"). PitWall AI determines the appropriate analysis, executes safe deterministic computations, and returns an interactive chart with the computation trace.
93: 
94: **Why this priority**: Covers the long tail of user questions that cannot be anticipated. Requires the most flexible analysis pipeline but builds on the same SQL and Python execution infrastructure.
95: 
96: **Independent Test**: Can be tested by submitting diverse custom queries and verifying that every returned chart has a valid computation trace and accurate numbers.
97: 
98: **Acceptance Scenarios**:
99: 
100: 1. **Given** the user asks "What is the average pit stop duration per team in 2023?", **When** the system processes the request, **Then** it generates the appropriate SQL query, executes it, and renders a bar chart with team-colored bars showing average pit stop durations, with the SQL query visible in the Engineering Trace.
101: 2. **Given** the user asks a question that requires combining historical and telemetry data, **When** the system detects the cross-domain query, **Then** it clearly labels which data comes from the historical SQL domain and which from the telemetry domain.
102: 
103: ---
104: 
105: ### User Story 7 - Live Progress Streaming & 2018 Boundary Explanation (Priority: P3)
106: 
107: While any analysis is loading, the user sees a step-by-step streaming progress feed showing what PitWall AI is doing (e.g., "Loading FastF1 session data…", "Executing SQL query…", "Computing braking deltas…"). When a user asks for car telemetry from before 2018, the system gracefully explains the data boundary.
108: 
109: **Why this priority**: Telemetry loading can take several seconds. Streaming progress prevents user frustration and builds trust in the computation pipeline. The 2018 boundary explanation prevents confusion.
110: 
111: **Independent Test**: Can be tested by timing a telemetry-heavy request and confirming that progress messages appear before the final result, and by asking for pre-2018 telemetry to verify the boundary explanation.
112: 
113: **Acceptance Scenarios**:
114: 
115: 1. **Given** the user submits a telemetry comparison request, **When** the data is loading, **Then** the UI streams status messages (e.g., "Loading 2023 Belgian GP Qualifying session…", "Extracting VER fastest lap…", "Slicing Eau Rouge corridor…") in real time before the final chart appears.
116: 2. **Given** the user asks "Show me Schumacher's telemetry at the 2004 Italian GP", **When** the system detects this is before 2018, **Then** it displays a clear explanation: "Car telemetry data is available from the 2018 season onwards. For 2004 and earlier seasons, I can provide historical race results, lap times, and championship standings."
117: 
118: ---
119: 
120: ### User Story 8 - Winner Prediction (Priority: P3)
121: 
122: A user asks "Who will win at Monza this year?" or "Who's the championship favorite?" PitWall AI analyzes recent form data for teams and drivers — recent race results, qualifying performance, circuit-specific history — and presents a prediction with confidence factors, all grounded in computed statistics, not LLM opinion.
123: 
124: **Why this priority**: Prediction adds a forward-looking engagement dimension. However, it must be built on the verified historical analytics pipeline and clearly communicated as a data-driven projection, not a guarantee.
125: 
126: **Independent Test**: Can be tested by verifying that every statistic cited in the prediction output traces back to a SQL query or computed metric, and that the confidence factors are based on explicit criteria.
127: 
128: **Acceptance Scenarios**:
129: 
130: 1. **Given** the user asks "Who will win the next race at Silverstone?", **When** the system processes the request, **Then** it displays a ranked prediction with percentage-based confidence scores, backed by explicit factors (recent form, circuit history, qualifying pace), each with a traceable SQL query or computation in the Engineering Trace.
131: 2. **Given** insufficient recent data exists for a meaningful prediction, **When** the system detects this, **Then** it states that the prediction confidence is low and explains what data is missing.
132: 
133: ---
134: 
135: ### Edge Cases
136: 
137: - What happens when a user asks for telemetry from a sprint session that only had a sprint qualifying format (post-2023 format changes)?
138: - How does the system handle a wet-weather qualifying session where some drivers did not set a representative lap?
139: - What happens when two team colors are nearly identical on the dark HUD background (e.g., AlphaTauri blue vs Williams blue)?
140: - How does the system respond when a user asks about a future season for which no data exists yet?
141: - What happens when FastF1 session data is temporarily unavailable or corrupted? The system serves from local cache if available (indicating staleness), retries 1–2 times on transient errors, and fails with a clear error only if no cache exists.
142: - How does the system handle corner nicknames that apply to different corners at different circuits (e.g., if a nickname is ambiguous)?
143: - What happens when a race was red-flagged and restarted, producing two sets of stint data?
144: - How does the system handle historical races with incomplete or missing timing data (pre-1980s)?
145: 
146: ## Clarifications
147: 
148: ### Session 2026-11-22
149: 
150: - Q: Does PitWall AI require user authentication to access, or is it open public? → A: Authenticated — users must sign in (email, OAuth, or similar) to access the app.
151: - Q: Is PitWall AI single-shot Q&A or multi-turn conversation with memory? → A: Multi-turn within a session (rolling summary + last 4–6 turns verbatim), stateless across sessions.
152: - Q: What safety boundary constrains ad-hoc Python execution for custom analysis? → A: LLM-generated Python runs in a restricted sandbox with no filesystem access, no network access, and a strict execution timeout.
153: - Q: When FastF1 is unavailable at runtime, what is the fallback behavior? → A: Cache-first fallback — serve from local cache if available (indicating data freshness to the user), plus 1–2 retries on transient timeouts before failing with an error if no cache exists.
154: - Q: What is the target number of concurrent authenticated users for initial release? → A: 5–10 concurrent users.
155: 
156: ## Requirements *(mandatory)*
157: 
158: ### Functional Requirements
159: 
160: - **FR-001**: System MUST accept natural-language questions about Formula 1 and determine whether the question requires historical SQL data, car telemetry data, or both.
161: - **FR-002**: System MUST generate and execute deterministic DuckDB SQL queries for all historical data questions (1950–2024+). No number may be produced from LLM memory.
162: - **FR-003**: System MUST load and process car telemetry via FastF1 for all telemetry-based analyses (2018+ seasons only). When FastF1 is unavailable, the system MUST first attempt to serve from local cache (indicating data freshness to the user). If no cache exists, the system MUST retry 1–2 times on transient timeouts before returning an explicit error message.
163: - **FR-004**: System MUST render corner-by-corner telemetry comparisons showing synchronized Speed, Speed Delta, Throttle, Brake, and Gear panels for a user-specified corner (by turn number or famous nickname).
164: - **FR-005**: System MUST compute five corner metrics for every corner comparison: braking point delta, apex minimum speed, lowest gear, full-throttle pickup point, and corner time delta.
165: - **FR-006**: System MUST render a zoomed GPS track mini-map for corner comparisons, colored by which driver is faster through each segment.
166: - **FR-007**: System MUST default to Qualifying fastest laps when the user does not specify a session type for telemetry comparisons.
167: - **FR-008**: System MUST render full-lap telemetry overlays comparing two drivers across an entire lap.
168: - **FR-009**: System MUST chart tyre stint degradation, filtering out pit-in/pit-out laps and Safety Car laps, with traces colored by compound type.
169: - **FR-010**: System MUST render race position evolution charts showing each driver's position per lap, colored by official team colors, with pit-stop and Safety Car annotations.
170: - **FR-011**: System MUST handle ad-hoc cross-metric questions by generating safe deterministic Python or SQL computations and returning interactive charts. All LLM-generated Python code MUST execute inside a restricted sandbox with no filesystem access, no network access, and a strict execution timeout. If execution exceeds the timeout or attempts a forbidden operation, the system MUST return an error rather than a partial or unsafe result.
171: - **FR-012**: System MUST stream step-by-step progress messages to the UI while loading data and performing computations.
172: - **FR-013**: System MUST gracefully explain the 2018 telemetry boundary when a user requests car telemetry from an earlier season, and suggest available historical alternatives.
173: - **FR-014**: System MUST display a collapsible Engineering Trace panel alongside every result, showing the exact SQL query or telemetry parameters used.
174: - **FR-015**: System MUST use official F1 team colors (sourced from a canonical registry, not hardcoded) for all driver and team visual encodings, correct for the depicted season.
175: - **FR-016**: System MUST display session and lap metadata (Grand Prix name, year, session type, lap number, driver code, compound, weather conditions) on every data visualization.
176: - **FR-017**: System MUST render all telemetry visualizations on a dark HUD background (#0B0F17) with WCAG AA compliant text contrast.
177: - **FR-018**: System MUST provide winner and championship predictions grounded in computed statistics (recent form, circuit history, qualifying pace) with explicit confidence factors and traceable computation sources.
178: - **FR-019**: System MUST provide race-engineer style natural-language commentary on telemetry comparisons, grounded exclusively in the computed metrics.
179: - **FR-020**: System MUST correctly identify corners by famous nickname (e.g., Copse, Eau Rouge, Maggotts-Becketts, 130R, Parabolica) and map them to the correct track coordinates.
180: - **FR-021**: System MUST slice telemetry data for corner comparisons using an entry-apex-exit window of approximately ±200 meters around the corner reference point.
181: - **FR-022**: All interactive charts MUST support hover tooltips, zoom, and pan interactions.
182: - **FR-023**: System MUST require user authentication (sign-in) before granting access to any feature. Unauthenticated users MUST be redirected to a login screen.
183: - **FR-024**: System MUST support multi-turn conversation within a session, allowing follow-up questions that reference previous context (e.g., "Now show his teammate's lap"). Context MUST be maintained via a rolling summary plus the last 4–6 turns verbatim.
184: - **FR-025**: System MUST be stateless across sessions — no conversation history persists after a session ends. Each new session starts with a clean context.
185: 
186: ### Key Entities
187: 
188: - **Driver**: A Formula 1 driver identified by code, full name, nationality, and career span. Associated with one or more Constructors per season.
189: - **Constructor**: A Formula 1 team identified by name, nationality, and active seasons. Associated with one or two Drivers per season and a team color palette per season.
190: - **Race / Grand Prix**: A race event identified by name, circuit, season year, round number, and date. Contains Results, Lap Times, Pit Stops, and optionally Telemetry Sessions.
191: - **Session**: A specific track session (FP1, FP2, FP3, Qualifying, Sprint, Race) within a Grand Prix weekend. For 2018+ sessions, may contain car Telemetry data.
192: - **Telemetry Lap**: A single timed lap within a Session, containing channel data (Speed, Throttle, Brake, Gear, RPM, DRS, X/Y/Z position) at sub-second intervals.
193: - **Corner / Turn**: A defined section of a Circuit identified by turn number and optionally a famous nickname. Used as the reference point for entry-apex-exit slicing.
194: - **Stint**: A contiguous run of laps on the same tyre compound within a Race, bounded by pit stops or session start/end.
195: - **User Account**: An authenticated identity with a unique identifier, used to gate access to PitWall AI. Associated with a login method (email/password, OAuth, or similar).
196: - **Conversation Session**: A single continuous interaction session between a user and PitWall AI. Contains a rolling summary of earlier turns plus the last 4–6 turns verbatim for context resolution. Not persisted after the session ends.
197: - **Prediction**: A data-driven projection of race or championship outcomes, containing ranked candidates, confidence scores, and the statistical factors that produced them.
198: 
199: ## Success Criteria *(mandatory)*
200: 
201: ### Measurable Outcomes
202: 
203: - **SC-001**: Users receive accurate answers to historical F1 questions within 5 seconds for SQL-based queries. Accuracy is verified against official FIA records with 100% correctness for factual lookups.
204: - **SC-002**: Corner-by-corner telemetry comparisons load and render within 15 seconds, including data retrieval, computation, and chart rendering.
205: - **SC-003**: Every user-facing number in every response traces back to a verifiable SQL query or deterministic computation — zero numbers produced from LLM memory (zero-hallucination guarantee).
206: - **SC-004**: 100% of telemetry visualizations render on the dark HUD background with correct team colors and WCAG AA text contrast.
207: - **SC-005**: The Engineering Trace panel is present and populated for 100% of data-bearing responses.
208: - **SC-006**: The system correctly explains the 2018 telemetry boundary 100% of the time when users request pre-2018 car telemetry, offering relevant historical alternatives.
209: - **SC-007**: Users can ask any historical F1 question spanning 1950–2024+ and receive a chart, table, or combined visualization — covering drivers, constructors, circuits, seasons, pit stops, and championship standings.
210: - **SC-008**: Automated pytest suites covering all features pass against real race data with no synthetic mocks for user-facing computations.
211: - **SC-009**: Winner predictions include explicit confidence factors and every cited statistic is traceable to a computed source.
212: - **SC-010**: Users experience streaming progress feedback for any operation that takes longer than 2 seconds.
213: 
214: ## Assumptions
215: 
216: - Users have a modern web browser with support for interactive charting (canvas/SVG rendering).
217: - The FastF1 library provides reliable access to telemetry data for 2018+ seasons; the system depends on FastF1's data availability and caching infrastructure.
218: - Historical race data (1950–2024+) is pre-loaded into a DuckDB database sourced from Ergast or equivalent official F1 data repositories.
219: - Corner nickname-to-coordinate mappings are maintained as a curated reference dataset within the application.
220: - The application requires authentication; all users must sign in before accessing any feature.
221: - The application targets 5–10 concurrent authenticated users for the initial release; high-concurrency scaling is out of scope for the initial version.
222: - Mobile-responsive design is a secondary concern; the primary interface targets desktop/laptop screens where telemetry charts are readable.
223: - The system does not provide real-time live timing during active race sessions; it analyzes completed sessions only.
224: - Winner predictions are explicitly framed as data-driven projections, not guarantees, and are based on historical and recent performance data only.

import re
from pathlib import Path

spec_path = Path("specs/001-pitwall-ai/spec.md")
plan_path = Path("specs/001-pitwall-ai/plan.md")
tasks_path = Path("specs/001-pitwall-ai/tasks.md")
dm_path = Path("specs/001-pitwall-ai/data-model.md")
const_path = Path(".specify/memory/constitution.md")

spec_text = spec_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
plan_text = plan_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
tasks_text = tasks_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
dm_text = dm_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
const_text = const_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")

# Extract citations
citations = re.findall(r"\(cites\s+`data-model\.md`:\s*([^\)]+)\)", tasks_text)
cited_items = set()
for c in citations:
    for item in c.split(","):
        cleaned = item.strip().strip("`")
        if cleaned:
            cited_items.add(cleaned)

print(f"Total cited items in tasks: {len(cited_items)}")
for item in sorted(cited_items):
    print("  ", item)

# Tables in data-model
tables = re.findall(r"#### (\w+)\s*\n\n\| Column \| Type \| Nullable \| Description \|\n\|[-|\s]+\|\n((?:\| [^|\n]+ \| [^|\n]+ \| [^|\n]+ \| [^|\n]+ \|\n)+)", dm_text)
constrained_table_fields = []
for tname, tbody in tables:
    for line in tbody.strip().splitlines():
        col, ctype, nullable, desc = [x.strip() for x in line.split("|")[1:-1]]
        if nullable == "NO" or "PK" in desc or "FK" in desc:
            constrained_table_fields.append((f"{tname}.{col}", f"{ctype}, Nullable: {nullable}, {desc}"))

print(f"\nConstrained table fields ({len(constrained_table_fields)}):")
unref = []
for f, info in constrained_table_fields:
    is_cited = f in cited_items
    if not is_cited:
        unref.append((f, info))

print(f"Referenced: {len(constrained_table_fields) - len(unref)} / {len(constrained_table_fields)}")
if unref:
    print("Unreferenced constrained fields:")
    for f, info in unref:
        print(f"  {f} ({info})")

7: ## R1: LLM Orchestration Framework
8: 
9: **Decision**: Google ADK (`google-adk`) with Gemini 2.5 Flash
10: 
11: **Rationale**: Google ADK provides a structured agent framework with native tool-calling, function declarations, and streaming support. Gemini 2.5 Flash offers fast inference with strong code-generation capabilities at low cost — ideal for SQL/Python authoring where the model writes code rather than performing arithmetic. The ADK's tool-routing pattern naturally enforces the zero-hallucination boundary: the LLM selects and parameterizes tools, but never computes numbers itself.
12: 
13: **Alternatives Considered**:
14: - LangChain/LangGraph: More ecosystem momentum but heavier abstraction; ADK is leaner and natively aligned with Gemini.
15: - OpenAI function calling: Would require a separate API key and billing; ADK keeps the stack on a single provider.
16: - Direct Gemini API calls: Would work but ADK adds tool declaration, session management, and streaming helpers that reduce boilerplate.
17: 
18: ## R2: Historical Data Storage
19: 
20: **Decision**: DuckDB with Kaggle CSV ingestion, `\N` → NULL normalization, read-only SQL views
21: 
22: **Rationale**: DuckDB is an embedded analytical database that requires zero infrastructure (no server process). It excels at analytical queries over CSV-scale data (~100K–1M rows). The `\N` sentinel used in Ergast/Kaggle CSVs must be normalized to SQL NULL at ingestion time to prevent silent type errors. Read-only views (`v_race_results`, `v_qualifying`, `v_pit_stops`, `v_driver_standings`) provide a stable query interface and prevent accidental writes — enforcing Constitution Principle I (all numbers from SQL).
23: 
24: **Alternatives Considered**:
25: - SQLite: Lacks analytical query optimizations (columnar scans, vectorized execution) that DuckDB provides.
26: - PostgreSQL: Requires a running server process; overkill for 5–10 concurrent users with static historical data.
27: - Pandas-only: No SQL interface for the LLM to generate queries against; would require the LLM to write Python data manipulation code instead, increasing hallucination surface.
28: 
29: **Key Implementation Details**:
30: - Ingestion script reads all CSVs from `data/kaggle_csvs/`, replaces `\N` strings with NULL during COPY.
31: - Views are created at startup via `CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW` statements.
32: - DuckDB connection is opened in read-only mode for query execution tools; write access only during initial ingestion.
33: 
34: ## R3: Car Telemetry Pipeline
35: 
36: **Decision**: FastF1 with persistent disk cache (`./data/fastf1_cache`) + NumPy 1-meter distance interpolation
37: 
38: **Rationale**: FastF1 is the de-facto Python library for accessing F1 telemetry data (2018+). Its built-in caching avoids re-downloading large session files. NumPy 1-meter distance interpolation resamples telemetry channels to a uniform spatial grid, which is essential for accurate corner slicing (±200m entry-apex-exit windows) and driver-to-driver comparison — you can't compare two drivers' speed at "the same point on track" without spatial alignment.
39: 
40: **Alternatives Considered**:
41: - Raw F1 timing API: No public stable API; FastF1 abstracts this.
42: - Time-based interpolation: Would misalign traces through corners where drivers have different speeds (and thus cover distance at different rates). Distance-based is correct for spatial comparisons.
43: 
44: **Key Implementation Details**:
45: - `fastf1.Cache.enable_cache('./data/fastf1_cache')` at app startup.

145: ### Read-Only SQL Views
146: 
147: #### v_race_results
148: 
149: Joins results + races + drivers + constructors + circuits + status. Provides a single denormalized view for all race result queries.
150: 
151: ```sql
152: CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW v_race_results AS
153: SELECT
154:     r.year, r.round, r.name AS grand_prix, r.date AS race_date,
155:     c.name AS circuit, c.country,
156:     d.code AS driver_code, d.forename, d.surname, d.nationality AS driver_nationality,
157:     con.name AS constructor, con.nationality AS constructor_nationality,
158:     res.grid, res.position, res.positionText, res.points, res.laps,
159:     res.time AS finish_time, res.milliseconds AS finish_ms,
160:     res.fastestLap, res.fastestLapTime, res.fastestLapSpeed,
161:     s.status
162: FROM results res
163: JOIN races r ON res.raceId = r.raceId
164: JOIN drivers d ON res.driverId = d.driverId
165: JOIN constructors con ON res.constructorId = con.constructorId
166: JOIN circuits c ON r.circuitId = c.circuitId
167: JOIN status s ON res.statusId = s.statusId;
168: ```
169: 
170: #### v_qualifying
171: 
172: ```sql
173: CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW v_qualifying AS
174: SELECT
175:     r.year, r.round, r.name AS grand_prix,
176:     d.code AS driver_code, d.forename, d.surname,
177:     con.name AS constructor,
178:     q.position, q.q1, q.q2, q.q3
179: FROM qualifying q
180: JOIN races r ON q.raceId = r.raceId
181: JOIN drivers d ON q.driverId = d.driverId
182: JOIN constructors con ON q.constructorId = con.constructorId;
183: ```
184: 
185: #### v_pit_stops
186: 
187: ```sql
188: CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW v_pit_stops AS
189: SELECT
190:     r.year, r.round, r.name AS grand_prix,
191:     d.code AS driver_code, d.surname,
192:     con.name AS constructor,
193:     ps.stop, ps.lap, ps.duration, ps.milliseconds AS duration_ms
194: FROM pit_stops ps
195: JOIN races r ON ps.raceId = r.raceId
196: JOIN drivers d ON ps.driverId = d.driverId
197: JOIN constructors con ON (
198:     SELECT res.constructorId FROM results res
199:     WHERE res.raceId = ps.raceId AND res.driverId = ps.driverId
200:     LIMIT 1
201: ) = con.constructorId;
202: ```
203: 
204: #### v_driver_standings
205: 
206: ```sql
207: CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW v_driver_standings AS
208: SELECT
209:     r.year, r.round, r.name AS grand_prix,
210:     d.code AS driver_code, d.forename, d.surname,
211:     ds.points, ds.position, ds.wins
212: FROM driver_standings ds
213: JOIN races r ON ds.raceId = r.raceId
214: JOIN drivers d ON ds.driverId = d.driverId;
215: ```

221: SELECT
222:     r.year, r.round, r.name AS grand_prix,

224:     cs.points, cs.position, cs.wins
225: FROM constructor_standings cs
226: JOIN races r ON cs.raceId = r.raceId
227: JOIN constructors con ON cs.constructorId = con.constructorId;
228: ```

import duckdb
import glob
import os
from pathlib import Path

csv_dir = Path("data/kaggle")
csv_files = list(csv_dir.glob("*.csv"))
print(f"Found {len(csv_files)} CSV files in {csv_dir}")

conn = duckdb.connect(":memory:")

for f in csv_files:
    tname = f.stem
    file_path = str(f).replace("\\", "/")
    query = f"""
    CREATE TABLE "{tname}" AS 
    SELECT * FROM read_csv('{file_path}', header=true, nullstr=['\\N', ''], auto_detect=true);
    """
    conn.execute(query)
    count = conn.execute(f'SELECT count(*) FROM "{tname}"').fetchone()[0]
    print(f"Table '{tname}': {count} rows")

# Check \N conversion on a table known to have \N like results (time, milliseconds, fastestLapSpeed)
null_check = conn.execute('SELECT count(*) FROM results WHERE milliseconds IS NULL').fetchone()[0]
print(f"results milliseconds IS NULL count: {null_check}")

# Test creating views
views_sql = """
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW v_race_results AS
SELECT
    r.year, r.round, r.name AS grand_prix, r.date AS race_date,
    c.name AS circuit, c.country,
    d.code AS driver_code, d.forename, d.surname, d.nationality AS driver_nationality,
    con.name AS constructor, con.nationality AS constructor_nationality,
    res.grid, res.position, res.positionText, res.points, res.laps,
    res.time AS finish_time, res.milliseconds AS finish_ms,
    res.fastestLap, res.fastestLapTime, res.fastestLapSpeed,
    s.status
FROM results res
JOIN races r ON res.raceId = r.raceId
JOIN drivers d ON res.driverId = d.driverId
JOIN constructors con ON res.constructorId = con.constructorId
JOIN circuits c ON r.circuitId = c.circuitId
JOIN status s ON res.statusId = s.statusId;

CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW v_qualifying AS
SELECT
    r.year, r.round, r.name AS grand_prix,
    d.code AS driver_code, d.forename, d.surname,
    con.name AS constructor,
    q.position, q.q1, q.q2, q.q3
FROM qualifying q
JOIN races r ON q.raceId = r.raceId
JOIN drivers d ON q.driverId = d.driverId
JOIN constructors con ON q.constructorId = con.constructorId;

CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW v_pit_stops AS
SELECT
    r.year, r.round, r.name AS grand_prix,
    d.code AS driver_code, d.surname,
    con.name AS constructor,
    ps.stop, ps.lap, ps.duration, ps.milliseconds AS duration_ms
FROM pit_stops ps
JOIN races r ON ps.raceId = r.raceId
JOIN drivers d ON ps.driverId = d.driverId
JOIN constructors con ON (
    SELECT res.constructorId FROM results res
    WHERE res.raceId = ps.raceId AND res.driverId = ps.driverId
    LIMIT 1
) = con.constructorId;

CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW v_driver_standings AS
SELECT
    r.year, r.round, r.name AS grand_prix,
    d.code AS driver_code, d.forename, d.surname,
    ds.points, ds.position, ds.wins
FROM driver_standings ds
JOIN races r ON ds.raceId = r.raceId
JOIN drivers d ON ds.driverId = d.driverId;

CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW v_constructor_standings AS
SELECT
    r.year, r.round, r.name AS grand_prix,
    con.name AS constructor, con.nationality AS constructor_nationality,
    cs.points, cs.position, cs.wins
FROM constructor_standings cs
JOIN races r ON cs.raceId = r.raceId
JOIN constructors con ON cs.constructorId = con.constructorId;
"""

for stmt in views_sql.strip().split(";"):
    stmt = stmt.strip()
    if stmt:
        conn.execute(stmt)

print("Views created successfully!")
for v in ["v_race_results", "v_qualifying", "v_pit_stops", "v_driver_standings", "v_constructor_standings"]:
    cnt = conn.execute(f"SELECT count(*) FROM {v}").fetchone()[0]
    print(f"View '{v}': {cnt} rows")

print("ALL VIEWS AND CSV INGESTION VERIFIED SUCCESSFULLY!")

"""
Views module for PitWall AI.
Defines the 5 curated read-only DuckDB SQL views for Formula 1 historical data.
"""

V_RACE_RESULTS_SQL = """
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW v_race_results AS
SELECT
    r.year, r.round, r.name AS grand_prix, r.date AS race_date,
    c.name AS circuit, c.country,
    d.code AS driver_code, d.forename, d.surname, d.nationality AS driver_nationality,
    con.name AS constructor, con.nationality AS constructor_nationality,
    res.grid, res.position, res.positionText, res.points, res.laps,
    res.time AS finish_time, res.milliseconds AS finish_ms,
    res.fastestLap, res.fastestLapTime, res.fastestLapSpeed,
    s.status
FROM results res
JOIN races r ON res.raceId = r.raceId
JOIN drivers d ON res.driverId = d.driverId
JOIN constructors con ON res.constructorId = con.constructorId
JOIN circuits c ON r.circuitId = c.circuitId
JOIN status s ON res.statusId = s.statusId;
"""

V_QUALIFYING_SQL = """
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW v_qualifying AS
SELECT
    r.year, r.round, r.name AS grand_prix,
    d.code AS driver_code, d.forename, d.surname,
    con.name AS constructor,
    q.position, q.q1, q.q2, q.q3
FROM qualifying q
JOIN races r ON q.raceId = r.raceId
JOIN drivers d ON q.driverId = d.driverId
JOIN constructors con ON q.constructorId = con.constructorId;
"""

V_PIT_STOPS_SQL = """
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW v_pit_stops AS
SELECT
    r.year, r.round, r.name AS grand_prix,
    d.code AS driver_code, d.surname,
    con.name AS constructor,
    ps.stop, ps.lap, ps.duration, ps.milliseconds AS duration_ms
FROM pit_stops ps
JOIN races r ON ps.raceId = r.raceId
JOIN drivers d ON ps.driverId = d.driverId
JOIN constructors con ON (
    SELECT res.constructorId FROM results res
    WHERE res.raceId = ps.raceId AND res.driverId = ps.driverId
    LIMIT 1
) = con.constructorId;
"""

V_DRIVER_STANDINGS_SQL = """
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW v_driver_standings AS
SELECT
    r.year, r.round, r.name AS grand_prix,
    d.code AS driver_code, d.forename, d.surname,
    ds.points, ds.position, ds.wins
FROM driver_standings ds
JOIN races r ON ds.raceId = r.raceId
JOIN drivers d ON ds.driverId = d.driverId;
"""

V_CONSTRUCTOR_STANDINGS_SQL = """
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW v_constructor_standings AS
SELECT
    r.year, r.round, r.name AS grand_prix,
    con.name AS constructor, con.nationality AS constructor_nationality,
    cs.points, cs.position, cs.wins
FROM constructor_standings cs
JOIN races r ON cs.raceId = r.raceId
JOIN constructors con ON cs.constructorId = con.constructorId;
"""

ALL_VIEWS_SQL = [
    ("v_race_results", V_RACE_RESULTS_SQL),
    ("v_qualifying", V_QUALIFYING_SQL),
